content: 1. Baseline laboratory evaluations, including hepatic enzyme levels, bilirubin, serum creatinine, a complete blood count, and a platelet count (or estimate), are recommended. However, these baseline tests are not necessary in pediatric patients unless a complicating condition is known or clinically suspected. 2. Patients undergoing therapy should be monitored at least monthly, with specific attention given to symptoms indicative of adverse reactions. Any abnormalities detected should prompt follow-up, including additional laboratory testing if required. 3. Routine laboratory monitoring for toxicity is generally unnecessary in individuals with normal baseline measurements. 4. There is limited information available regarding the intravenous compatibility of rifampin (injection) in the drug label. 5. In cases of overdose, symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, pruritus, headache, and increasing lethargy are likely to occur shortly after ingestion. Severe hepatic disease may lead to unconsciousness. Transient increases in liver enzymes and/or bilirubin may also be observed. 6. Overdose can cause brownish-red or orange discoloration of the skin, urine, sweat, saliva, tears, and feces, with the intensity of discoloration proportional to the amount ingested. 7. Hepatomegaly, potentially with tenderness, may develop within hours of a severe overdose. Bilirubin levels may rise, and jaundice can develop rapidly. Hepatic involvement is often more pronounced in patients with pre-existing liver dysfunction. 8. Other physical findings typically remain normal. Direct effects on the hematopoietic system, electrolyte levels, or acid-base balance are unlikely. 9. Facial or periorbital edema has been reported in pediatric patients. Hypotension, sinus tachycardia, ventricular arrhythmias, seizures, and cardiac arrest have been observed in some fatal cases. 10. The minimum acute lethal or toxic dose of rifampin is not well established. Nonfatal acute overdoses in adults have been reported with doses ranging from 9 to 12 grams, while fatal overdoses have occurred with doses between 14 and 60 grams. Alcohol use or a history of alcohol abuse was implicated in some of these cases. 11. Nonfatal overdoses in pediatric patients aged 1 to 4 years have been reported with doses of 100 mg/kg for one to two doses. 12. Intensive supportive measures should be implemented, and individual symptoms should be treated as they arise. The airway must be secured, and adequate respiratory exchange should be ensured. 13. Due to the likelihood of nausea and vomiting, gastric lavage within the first 2 to 3 hours after ingestion is preferable to inducing emesis. Following gastric evacuation, the administration of activated charcoal slurry into the stomach may help absorb any remaining drug in the gastrointestinal tract. 14. Antiemetic medications may be required to manage severe nausea and vomiting. 15. Active diuresis, with careful monitoring of fluid intake and output, can aid in promoting drug excretion. 16. In severe cases, extracorporeal hemodialysis may be necessary. If unavailable, peritoneal dialysis combined with forced diuresis can be employed. 17. Rifampin inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase activity in susceptible Mycobacterium tuberculosis organisms. It specifically interacts with bacterial RNA polymerase without affecting the mammalian enzyme. 18. Organisms resistant to rifampin are likely to exhibit resistance to other rifamycins. Resistance can emerge rapidly due to single-step mutations in the DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Susceptibility testing should be performed if persistent positive cultures are observed. 19. Rifampin demonstrates bactericidal activity in vitro against slow and intermittently growing M. tuberculosis organisms. It is active against most strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Neisseria meningitidis in both in vitro and clinical infections. 20. Rifampin has shown activity against aerobic Gram-positive microorganisms such as Staphylococcus aureus (including methicillin-resistant strains, MRSA) and Staphylococcus epidermidis, as well as aerobic Gram-negative microorganisms like Haemophilus influenzae. It is also active against Mycobacterium leprae. 21. β-lactamase production does not affect rifampin's activity. 22. Prior to initiating therapy, appropriate specimens should be collected for identification of the infecting organism and in vitro susceptibility testing. 23. For Mycobacterium tuberculosis, two standardized in vitro susceptibility testing methods are available to determine drug resistance. After three weeks of incubation, MIC99 values are calculated by comparing the growth of organisms in drug-containing media to control cultures. Resistance is indicated if mycobacterial growth in the presence of the drug is at least 1% of the growth in the control culture.
